facts.claim: Lissie's "Dragula" is a cover of Rob Zombie's song, made for the horror film Haunt.
The song is credited as written by Rob Zombie and Scott Humphrey and performed by Lissie in the Haunt soundtrack listing.
Lionboy Records released the cover as a digital single on September 13, 2019, the same day Haunt opened.
Lissie said she was honored that the Haunt directors asked her to cover the song. She said they come from her hometown area, the Quad Cities.
Lissie thanked Lance at Humans Win! Recording Studio for creating the track with her.
Haunt directors Scott Beck and Bryan Woods said they had wanted to work with Lissie for years. They said she crafted the cover with Lance Conrad at Humans Win! Recording Studio.
Her cover plays over the end credits of Haunt and is a softer, slower, acoustic take on the original.
Haunt is written and directed by Scott Beck and Bryan Woods, the writers of A Quiet Place, and was executive produced by Eli Roth.
Lissie (Elisabeth Maurus) was born in 1982 in Rock Island, Illinois. Her debut album Catching a Tiger came out in 2010, and her 2018 album Castles was a UK Top Ten record.
Lissie also appeared in Twin Peaks season 3, performing "Wild West", and she released a covers EP, Thank You To The Flowers, in 2020.

research.lineage: A stripped-back, ethereal acoustic reinterpretation of a 1998 industrial-metal classic, in the tradition of slowed-down cover versions used over horror-film end credits, coming from a Midwestern folk-rock/Americana singer-songwriter.

draft:
**Dragula** was built to stomp. In Lissie's hands it glides. The words haven't changed. A dead thing still narrates, still goes digging through ditches and burning through witches, still slams into the back of its hot rod. But the voice delivering them is clear, strong and a little breathy, holding each note long with a vibrato that widens as it goes. The menace hasn't been removed. It's been made to sound beautiful, and that's harder to shake.

The song is Rob Zombie's, written with Scott Humphrey, and Lissie recorded it for Haunt, the horror film by Scott Beck and Bryan Woods, the writers of A Quiet Place. Her version plays over the end credits, a softer, slower take on the original. It belongs to a tradition horror fans know well: once the screaming is done, the familiar song comes back hushed and strange, and the dread lingers into the lights coming up. The job has a hometown thread too. Beck and Woods come from the Quad Cities, the same area as Lissie, who was born in Rock Island, Illinois. She said she was honored they asked, and they said they'd wanted to work with her for years. She built the track with Lance Conrad at Humans Win! Recording Studio.

The arrangement stays out of the way. A bass holds simple, sustained notes. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords with some reverb on them. The drums keep a steady kick-and-snare pulse that moves the song forward without hurrying it. The production is polished and open, with room around every instrument, and there are no harmonies, so the single voice carries everything. That plainness is the trick. Nothing in the sound winks at you.

Zombie's lyrics are pure monster brag, a catalog of things the narrator has become: the sky, the pool, the rat. "Dead I am the sky, watchin' angels cry" sounds gloating when it's barked. Sung this sustained and melodic, it sounds closer to grief, or to a calm that's scarier than grief. The best line is "Tender is the fur, dyin' as you purr," and Lissie seems to have built the whole cover around it, tenderness and killing in the same breath, neither one cancelling the other. The final stretch repeats the coaxing "do it baby" and the command "Burn like an animal," and a voice this warm turns the order into an invitation. That's the unsettling part. The narrator isn't raging. It's enjoying itself, and it wants company.

The cover lets you feel what a monster might feel from the inside, unhurried and almost loving, and the sweetness is what keeps it in your head after the credits roll.
